title: Evening Lantern: Prefill + KV Cache Micro-Notes
content:
Context and purpose:
A short evening write-up from the prefill/kv-batching micro-lab. Intended to be a compact record of the small experiments we ran late today, the surprising observations, and the immediate follow-ups for the Monday triage. Treat as operational field-notes rather than a formal postmortem.

High-level summary (TL;DR):
- Tested a lightweight kernel handshake patch (PR 812) that defers slot allocation for short-lived chat sessions; reduced median p99 prefill latency for 16-token prefixes by ~18%.
- Observed a KV cache eviction amplification when micro-batches from spike traffic interleave with long-running streams; leads to 2–4% SLA blips in synthetic load tests.
- Validated a quick heuristic: prefer soft-evict on prefix-hit > 0.9 and demote slots instead of immediate eviction; cut synthetic miss storms by half in the lab.

What we actually ran:
1) Kernel handshake patch (branch: handshake-defer)
   - What: delay kernel slot handshake until first real token compute for sessions < 64 tokens expected (heuristic: upfront length hint or user-level metadata).
   - Why: avoid allocating expensive KV-backed slots for very short requests, reduce slot churn and kernel context switches.
   - Measurements (local rig, Ampere A1-equivalent):
     * baseline median prefill time (16-token prefixes): 42 ms
     * post-patch median: 34 ms
     * p95: 98 ms -> 83 ms
     * p99: 220 ms -> 182 ms
   - Notes: latency gains concentrated on low-LLM-seq workloads; no meaningful throughput change for long sequences. 1 flaky run where p99 spiked to 260 ms, correlates with GC pause in the node running the allocator.

2) KV cache eviction amplification test
   - Scenario: interleaved traffic with two cohorts: short bursts (avg 20 tokens) + streaming sessions (avg 1k tokens).
   - Observation: streaming sessions touch large KV namespaces and cause repeated evictions of shards used by burst cohort; burst cohort then experiences cache-miss cascades when a batch arrives and tries to prefill.
   - Measured effect: miss rate for burst cohort increased from 7% -> 22% during synthetic storm window. End-user p90 token latency regressed by ~12% in that window.

3) Quick mitigation: demote-not-evict heuristic
   - Implementation: when eviction would remove keys with recent prefix-hit ratio > 0.9, mark them as demoted (lower eviction priority) and try to pickle to shadow cache if available, otherwise schedule background compaction.
   - Result: miss rate during storm window fell from 22% -> 11% in lab. CPU overhead +0.9% (measured on controller).

Open questions and anomalies:
- Why did the handshake-defer patch cause a single high p99 run? Investigate allocator GC timings and whether defer increases burst allocation at a later point that transiently contends with the GC.
- Shadow cache warming: background pickle still competes with normal prefill work under high IO; should we rate-limit pickles? Need to simulate higher IO-bound disks.
- Demotion TTL: current heuristic uses a static 5m demotion window. Is that optimal for mixed workloads? A sliding demotion tied to cohort churn might be better.

Action items (who / by when):
- Marco: attach allocator GC trace for the 2026-03-21 23:12 run and correlate with kernel handshake timings; due Tue 2026-03-23.
- Priya: run shadow-cache pickle stress with an IO-bound emulation (throttle to 100 MB/s) and report CPU/IO contention metrics; due Wed 2026-03-24.
- Jon: prototype adaptive demotion TTL that increases with observed cohort churn; quick PoC in branch demotion-adaptive; due Fri 2026-03-26.
- Aisha: prepare a short canary rollout plan for PR 812 (handshake-defer) with a fallback gate and observability hooks; draft due Mon 2026-03-22 EOD.

Operational runbook notes (short):
- Canary gate for handshake-defer: start at 0.5% of sessions, keep for 1 hour, monitor prefill p50/p95/p99 and KV miss rate. If p99 increases >10% over baseline or KV miss rate increases >5% abort and rollback.
- Temp mitigation for live storm: enable demote-not-evict flag cluster-wide; requires feature-flag flip and monitor for CPU + IO.

Decisions and tradeoffs discussed:
- Defer handshake trades slightly increased cold-start for very short sessions (one extra small scheduling hop) for lower systemic churn and fewer p99 outliers across the fleet. Team consensus: worth canarying.
- Demote-not-evict increases controller CPU and complexity but avoids cascaded miss storms. Prefer conservative rollout and measurement.

Notes to the follow-on retro:
- Capture both synthetic load and replayed production traces: synthetic gives repeatability, but a single production replay exposed the GC/handshake spike. Save those traces in the experiment bucket.
- Add a short write-up on how prefill heuristics interact with admission control; possible follow-up to tie demotion TTL to admission-control signals.

Quick links and observability pointers used tonight:
- perf dashboard (prefill latency): dashboards/redwood/prefill-latency
- KV metrics: metrics.kvcache.{misses,evictions,demotes}
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/812
- Jira: RT-4213 (handshake-defer), RT-4290 (kv-demote-heuristic)

Casual notes (notes-to-self style):
- The evening lab felt like chasing a slippery artifact — repeatedly reproducing the eviction cascade required the exact burst-stream interleave. Consider adding a small harness that can lock cohort timing deterministicly.
- The demote idea probably buys us time for smarter admission/routing decisions — but bigger wins will be from admission control that avoids giving large streams the same slot type as burst cohorts.

If anything here looks off or you'd like a deeper perf table, ping me on #serving-runtime (thread: #evening-lantern) and I can drop the raw CSVs.

— Aisha
